svg.title: Literary criticism is an argument about an argument
svg.desc: Three stacked layers on the left. The bottom layer is the text itself, a novel, poem, play or film, which the critic reads but which you never see except in quotation. The middle layer is the critic's interpretation, a claim that some feature of the text signifies something beyond its surface, which is the thesis and the thing every question is really about. The top layer is your job: not whether the interpretation is right, but whether the argument works on its own terms. On the right, the three-step chain by which strong criticism uses evidence. Step one, identify a specific textual feature, for example the sentences grow shorter and break off as the chapters proceed. Step two, describe what that feature does in the text, for example the syntax enacts a loss of control rather than describing one. Step three, argue that this produces or exemplifies the claimed meaning, for example form and content become inseparable, which is the interpretation. A panel notes that weak arguments quote and then restate the thesis, skipping step two or step three, and that when a question asks what is missing from an argument or what would strengthen it, the missing link is usually step two. A footer warns against the single most common wrong turn: asking whether the interpretation is right. Two critics can read the same lines as celebration and as irony, and both can be arguing well. The question is never whether you agree, but whether the evidence does the work the critic says it does.
svg.text: Literary criticism is an argument about an argument
The passage is never about the novel. It is about what a critic claims the novel does — and your job is the third layer.
YOUR JOB
Not: is this reading right? But: does the
argument work on its own terms?
THE CRITIC'S INTERPRETATION
A claim that some feature of the text signifies
something beyond its surface. This is the thesis
— and what every question is really about.
THE TEXT
The novel, poem, play or film. You never see it
except in quotation.
1 · IDENTIFY
a specific textual feature
“the sentences grow shorter and break off as the chapters
proceed”
2 · DESCRIBE
what that feature does in the text
“the syntax enacts a loss of control rather than
describing one”
3 · ARGUE
that this produces the claimed meaning
“form and content become inseparable” — the interpretation
What a weak argument leaves out
Weak criticism quotes and then restates the thesis, skipping
step 2 or step 3. When a question asks what is missing from an
argument, or what would most strengthen it, the absent link is
almost always step 2 — the account of what the feature
actually does. A quotation that is never unpacked supports
nothing.
The wrong question
“But is this reading right?” Two critics can take the same
lines as celebration and as irony and both be arguing
well. Ask only whether the evidence does the work the
critic says it does.
